This book was initially planned to be a second edition of his Language, Meaning and Context.
However, it turned out to be a successor and replacement, treating topics missing in the earlier volume and written in a different style.
By 'linguistic semantics', Lyons means the study of meaning systematically encoded in the vocabulary and grammar of natural language.
Thus, linguistic semantics is a branch of linguistics; semantic issues that relate more to philosophy belong to philosophical semantics.
Accordingly, Lyons devotes limited space to philosophical problems while cautioning that nobody can appreciate modern linguistic semantics without some acquaintance with its philosophical groundwork.
According to Lyons, the book can be used as a textbook for introductory semantics courses in departments of linguistics.
For those familiar with various key issues in semantics, the book is enjoyable as it raises interesting points and asks stimulating questions.
However, beginners may be unsettled by the lack of exercises and the verbose writing style.
LSAI consists of several parts, each followed by chapters comprising it.
Part 1 deals with the Herculean question of semantics: what is meaning?
It introduces the usual distinctions between language and speech, langue and parole, competence and performance, form and meaning, sentences and utterances.
Part 2 focuses on lexical meaning, discussing words as expressions and the fundamental distinction of tokens vs. types.
It studies homonymy, polysemy, and synonymy, along with techniques to define the meaning of words.
The final chapter hints at the notion of compositionality and studies propositional entailment.
Part 3 considers sentence meaning, discussing the verifiability principle and implications in natural language utterances.
It also covers the meaning of interrogative, imperative, and exclamative sentences, in addition to declaratives.
Part 4, based on J. L. Austin's theory of speech acts, includes notable chapters on context.
Lyons reviews the role of context using Paul Grice's accounts of conversational implicature and the principle of cooperation.
Despite its shortcomings, such as limited attention to contemporary theories like Government and Binding Theory, the book is commendable.
Writing books is risky business; Lyons's work does not fall but leaves much to be desired.
While there are no obvious 'conceptos', the book provides a good introduction to linguistic semantics.
Most of the work that has gone into compiling English-language corpora since the pioneering Brown Corpus in the 1960s has been devoted to American or British English.
But Britain and the USA are not the only English-speaking countries.
The International Corpus of English (ICE), an enterprise initiated by Sidney Greenbaum in 1989, aims to develop a co-ordinated collection of 'World Englishes'.
When complete, ICE will contain a subcorpus for each of 18 countries or regions, in some of which English is the native language, while in others it is the common language of public life.
This book, containing 19 chapters by different participants in the ICE effort, is the first easily accessible survey of what is planned and what has been achieved.

Each ICE subcorpus is intended to resemble Brown and LOB in comprising 500 samples each of 2000 words, but half the samples will be speech, and the written samples will include manuscript as well as printed material.
The period represented will be the 1990s, though some teams have had to ignore the original planned cutoff of 1994.
Samples are intended to represent the 'educated' or 'standard' English of the respective country, but this is a highly problematic concept.
The book contains many references to debates about whether countries such as Nigeria can be described as having a separate local standard variety of English.
Like Brown and LOB, the ICE subcorpora aim to allot subsets of their samples to different genres in a systematic way.
For the British subcorpus, the work of adding wordtags and parse structure is evidently well advanced.
There is plenty of information given about the semiautomatic techniques being used to carry this out.
These coding schemes are unrelated to the schemes used by other well-known English-language corpus projects.
Considerable ICE resources have evidently been used to create software systems for helping users of the completed subcorpora execute tasks such as producing concordances.
In practice, there are usually two possibilities when one wants to exploit corpus data.
Often, one wants to put very obvious and simple questions to the corpus; in that case, it is usually possible to get answers via general-purpose Unix commands.
The final chapter by Mark Huckvale and Alex Fang explores the interaction between grammar and prosodic phonology.
Real discoveries have been made, and many more can be expected from this very promising research avenue.
ICE is not really a single project; it is a loose federation of disparate and widely-scattered research groups.
The book demonstrates that analogical methods are feasible and thus worthy of further research.
It will be of interest to anyone working in computational linguistics.
We describe an experimental approach toward implementing a commonsense microtheory for buying and selling.
Our prototype system characterizes how intelligent agents hold items and money, how they buy and sell items, and the way money and items are transferred.

The ontology of the system includes money (cash, check, credit card), agents (people, organizations), items (movable, real estate, service), barter, and the notions of transfer, loan, buying by installments, profit, and loss.
Some years ago, Mademoiselle Zélie, a singer, made a professional tour and gave a concert in the Society Islands.
In exchange for her performance, she received a share of the receipts that consisted of livestock and fruit, which illustrates the complexities of economic transactions.
Conventional wisdoms of buying and selling remain to be fully articulated.
Having intuitively perceived the function of money, we still need to order our perceptions precisely into a logical framework.
Money is a key instrument in buying and selling.
Agents can hold money in different forms: cash, bank accounts, and credit cards.
In every buying and selling process, an item is involved.
Items are classified as movable, real estate, and service, and can be further categorized as durables and nondurables.
The theory considers buying and selling as a money transfer and a corresponding item transfer.
For these transfers to occur, certain preconditions regarding the buyer and seller must hold.
Selling processes are generally profit-oriented.
If the sale price of an item is greater than its purchase price, the seller makes a profit.
Buyers can agree to pay for an item in installments.
This process involves a payment plan decided by both the seller and the buyer.
Borrowing can be defined as taking or receiving something for a certain time, intending to return it.
Different types of lenders exist, including friends, banks, and usurers.
Barter is defined as the direct exchange of items of equal value without the use of currency.
It requires a double coincidence of wants, which is often difficult to achieve.
The implementation of the theory uses the Knowledge Engineering Environment (KEE) as a software development tool.
The system's inference mechanism is provided by a number of rule classes built into the KEE.
This paper summarized the implementation of a preliminary model for commonsense buying and selling.
We have built a preliminary microtheory for buying and selling and covered a part of the intuitive knowledge required for understanding these processes.
The idea of an oracle comes from ancient Greece.
In the mythical literature, this word had two uses: (i) the place where questions about the future were asked of the gods, and (ii) the priest (or priestess) who gave answers to such questions.
In our conception, oracles should correspond to information servers for the objects they represent, and one should be able to pose queries concerning an object to its oracle.
For example, the oracle related to one of the organizers of an international colloquium should be able to answer questions about that organizer.
We are not the first researchers grappling with the idea of having an oracle.
One of the earliest uses of oracles goes back to Turing machines.
In the analysis of the toughest problem in computer science, oracles were heavily used.

This has two implications: (i) a conclusion obtained via hypothetical oracles is not necessarily unique, and (ii) using oracles we may find answers to very difficult problems under the assumptions embedded in the oracle.
The issue of oracle appears not only in the theory of computation but also in practical fields of computer science such as computer networks and client-server systems.

The plan of this paper is as follows: we will review the emergence of oracles in Situation Theory, summarize the concept of relevance in Pragmatics, and interpret these works in the light of Situation Theory.
Situation Theory is a principled program to develop a unified theory of meaning and information content.
One of the most notable motivations of the theory is to provide a mathematical theory of meaning.
Barwise and Perry claim that for an expression to have meaning, it should convey information.
They develop a theory of situations and of meaning as a relation between situations.
The theory provides a system of abstract objects that makes it possible to describe the meaning of both expressions and mental states in terms of the information they carry about the external world.
Two major concepts of Situation Theory are infons and situations.

Infons are the basic informational units, denoted as <P, a1,..., an, i>, where P is an n-place relation, a1,..., an are objects appropriate for the respective argument places of P, and i is the polarity.
Situations are first-class citizens of the theory, defined intensionally.
A situation is considered to be a structured part of reality that an agent manages to pick out.
An abstract situation is defined as a set of infons.
One important paradigm behind Situation Theory is a schema of individuation, a way of carving the world into uniformities.
In this paper, we shall mainly deal with the philosophy behind the nature of information and the ways of gathering relevant information.
Devlin defines oracles as situations.
In his definition, he uses the notion of a set of issues to mean a collection of parametric infons which provides an information-theoretic framework for discussing the world.
By anchoring the parameters of an infon in this set, we obtain an item of information.
Using different sets of issues, we can talk about different aspects of the world.
For example, if we are talking about Korta in the context of a colloquium, we may include information relevant to his role as an organizer.
One of the vaguest concepts in Devlin's definition is the relevance of information.
The issue of relevance is a well-researched topic in various fields of computer science.
In Information Retrieval, the measurement of relevance is a major line of research.
There are various syntactical approaches to measure the relevance of a term to a document.
Psychological, epistemic, and semantical considerations are beginning to appear.
According to Park, the search criteria for any query should be set according to the users' criteria of relevance.
Hearst studies the issue from a Computer Science point of view, implementing a full text information retrieval system.
In this paper, we will base our arguments on Sperber and Wilson, where relevance is considered to be the psychological relevance of a proposition to a context.
According to them, a proposition is relevant to a context if it interacts in a certain way with the existing assumptions about the world.
In our situation-theoretic account of oracle, we first redefine what an oracle is.
Oracler(a) is the collection of information from the set of available situations which are relevant to an object a in the context F.
This definition can be used with a two-phase procedure in an application.
We first search over the existing situations for the occurrence of a.
The notion of context was first introduced to AI in a logicist framework by McCarthy.
Research on the topic was quite silent until the late eighties.

McCarthy offers three reasons for introducing a formal notion of context: it allows simple axiomatizations, allows us to use specific vocabulary, and enables AI systems to transcend the context they are in.
In this paper, we have tried to give an outline and highlights of our research on context and the relevance of information.
While doing this, we have used the idea of oracle to broaden our view of the subject.
Our approach is similar to the human's way of measuring relevance.
We employ a formalization of context within Situation Theory.
Using our formalization of context together with Relevance Theory might be beneficial.
To the initial onlooker, punctuation marks and topic/focus structure of an orthographic sentence seem to be unrelated.
However, recent linguistic and computational research in punctuation have suggested that there may be interesting consequences of punctuation for the semantics of discourse.
Nunberg has suggested that the contributions of punctuation can be studied by means of a linguistic characterization of underlying categories and attached constraints.
Dale has observed that many uses of certain marks (e.g., comma, colon, semicolon, dash(es), parentheses) act as signals of discourse structure.
In this paper, we concentrate on em-dash as our sample punctuation mark and investigate its effects on information structure, focus, and anaphora.
We take Discourse Representation Theory (DRT), an influential theory dealing with various discourse related phenomena, as our framework.
In particular, Asher's extension of DRT with Segmented Discourse Representation Structures (SDRSs) proves valuable for us.
SDRSs provide various mechanisms to represent discourse structure and constraints on those representations for the resolution of abstract entity anaphora.
We see SDRT as a valuable framework for exploring problems of punctuation in which informational characteristics of written text are central.
In Section 2, we examine how dashes act as typographical cues for the information structure in written English.
We then examine how anaphora resolution is affected between dash interpolated text adjuncts and other text.
In Section 3, we give the necessary extensions to SDRT to be able to model the observed data.
The following observations are due to examining around 500 randomly selected sentences with dash interpolations.
The sentences come from the Wall Street Journal, the British National Corpus (BNC), and SUSANNE.
Depending on their origin, they are marked W, B, and S, respectively.
One observation is that dash interpolations do cue a subset of discourse relations quite reliably.
By discourse relations, we mean those bindings that relate two units of text by means of coherence and rhetorical effects.
The distribution of discourse relations in dash interpolated sentences is not completely ad hoc and is worthy of special consideration.
Indeed, 56% of the relations are in the categories of Elaboration, Commentary, and Apposition.
The second observation that relates to an interesting use of dash interpolation is when it is used to denote focus-in a combination of the informational sense and the intonational sense.
Informational focus of a sentence is the informative (new) part of a sentence that makes a contribution to a hearer's mental store.
Some dashes do not disrupt the syntactic flow of the sentence.
This could indicate an extra level of emphasis on informational prominence, where an intonational focus would already be expected in spoken text.
If the dash interpolation comes at the end of the sentence it is usually more prominent information-wise than its mid-sentence counterparts.
Some styles of writing make repeated use of the above effect and employ dash interpolations for intonational focus to keep a vivid and striking pace throughout the document.
Even when they are part of informational focus, mid-sentence dash interpolations can be parenthetical and less prominent than other parts of the sentence.
In this section, we give three additions to SDRT based on our findings.
Here, we try to concentrate on the implications of dashed sentences.
We adopt the basic definitions of DRT and SDRT as they are given in Asher.

In DRT, a semantic representation structure called Discourse Representation Structure (DRS) is assigned to a discourse segment by a syntax-driven construction algorithm that proceeds sentence by sentence relative to the context created by the DRS built so far.

In SDRT, there is an additional level of discourse interpretation in the form of Segmented DRSs (SDRSs) which are constructed by default for each orthographic sentence and enter into discourse relations with each other forming a discourse structure.
From now on, we will take an SDRS as corresponding to a text-sentence, a text-clause or a text-phrase as justified by the dashes.
We add the following conditions: If certain discourse referents are not preferable for selection, they should be denoted as parenthetical.
Discourse referents that denote special intonational focus should be made more prominent.
The third modification takes into account the alternative wording effect of dash interpolations.

A more detailed study is being performed as to whether dashes and other semantically significant punctuation marks can provide defeasible cues for the discourse interpretation of punctuated orthographic sentences.

Such a characterization may also lead to their inclusion in the relevant computational modules such as the anaphora resolution component of an NLP system already accounting for punctuation at a syntactic level.
Extending SDRT (and DRT) with suitable triggering conditions is our main project.
We see our attempt as beneficial and contributing to the efforts for modifying DRT to cover sentences from corpora.
Gul A. Agha's Actors: A Model of Concurrent Computation in Distributed Systems is part of the MIT Press Series in Artificial Intelligence.
In the actor formalism, pioneered by Carl Hewitt, one perceives abstract computational agents, called actors, that are distributed in space.
Each actor has a mailbox and an associated behavior.
One actor can influence the actions of another actor only by sending it a communication.
An actor can send another actor a communication only when it knows the address of the second actor.
An actor can receive more than one message simultaneously.
The actor model achieves simultaneous communication through buffering, where a recipient's mailbox is always ready to receive messages.
The difference between actors and objects in object-oriented programming is significant.
Objects can be conceived as ancestors of actors because they represent individual data items and operations on them.
However, actors are more powerful than sequential processes and data flow systems.
Programming a collection of actors is challenging.
Parallel programming is generally hard, and the need for another programming language like actors might seem difficult to argue.
Message passing is fundamental to computation in actors, and the time complexity of communication may become the dominant factor in program execution.
Recent research into the ecology of computation views distributed computational systems as models of social, economic, and biological organizations.
The book addresses issues of open systems and the design of appropriate languages for such systems.
Agha's book is essential for understanding the problems in obtaining actual implementations of distributed computation.
It also discusses the design of languages for open systems.
The actor approach is about the future of computing.
A new source in actor literature is Concurrent Systems for Knowledge Processing: An Actor Perspective, edited by C. Hewitt and G. Agha.

Following the steps of Aczel's ground-breaking monograph which marked a departure from the common sense attributed to classical set theory, this new book offers an introduction to the revolutionary and fascinating topic of non-wellfounded sets.
Barwise's quest for an enrichment of the concept of set can be traced back to his pioneering project in situation theory and situation semantics.
Barwise and Perry had no qualms about the kind of metatheory they needed for their project, but they thought they had to deal with the problem of large collections.
Their approach is to work in a metatheory like the theory KPU, one that admits an interpretation in terms of finite objects.
However, it was soon realized that large collections are only one of the difficulties; a more intricate issue is that of wellfoundedness.
What unifies the preceding notions is their inherent circularity.
Historically, it has invariably been the case that circularity and mathematical rigor hardly go hand in hand.
The Axiom of Foundation of classical set theory prohibits circularity.
One of the most exciting areas of application for non-wellfounded sets is situation semantics.
Situations can occur as components of facts, leading to circular situations that contain facts about themselves.
VC consists of six parts which altogether comprise 21 chapters.
Part I introduces the subject in a nontechnical way and summarizes the background material on classical set theory.
Part II is arguably the most readable part of the book, studying circularity in computer science and philosophy.
Chapter 3 studies circularity in computer science, concluding with a discussion of self-replicating programs.
Chapter 4 introduces logical and semantic paradoxes, including the Conway Paradox.
Chapter 5 studies the Liar Paradox and Kripke's influential paper on circularity of reference.
Part III explains the universe of hypersets and presents the Anti-Foundation Axiom.
Chapter 7 studies the conditions under which two systems of equations have the same solution, introducing the concept of 'bisimulation'.
Parts V and VI develop methods of greatest fixed points, co-induction, and co-recursion using complex mathematics.
Chapters 20 and 21 provide philosophical views on ZFC and ZFA, along with open problems.
The intended audience includes pure mathematicians and researchers in philosophy, game theory, computer science, and artificial intelligence.
Barwise and Moss assume that the reader has enough training to follow the intricate proofs.
The book has numerous typos and errors, indicating a need for a corrected printing.
The web-based automatic bug notification form for reporting errors is a good initiative, but it may not be updated frequently.
In VC, Barwise and Moss explore set theory to exercise their mathematical talents.
The result is a thought-provoking book that may become a classic in the field.
Mind Design II is a substantial yet inexpensive book and would be an excellent choice for an 'AI & Philosophy' course, particularly at the graduate level.
The book is conceived as a sequel to Alan Ross Anderson's Minds and Machines, augmenting it and bringing it up to date.

The revised and enlarged successor of Mind Design consists of the following chapters: 1. What is Mind Design? (by John Haugeland), 2. Computing Machinery and Intelligence (by A. M. Turing), 3. True Believers: The Intentional Strategy and Why It Works (by Daniel C. Dennett), and others.
Chapters 4, 5, 6, and 7 are taken from Mind Design.
The following chapters of the original book are not included in Mind Design II.
Haugeland's choices were most fitting; Mind Design quickly became a classic and found a secure place for itself in philosophical and AI circles.
The essays included here were written after that work appeared, and most of them were directly or indirectly influenced by it.
Dennett's essay discusses the intentional stance, a strategy for predicting behavior.
Dreyfus's critique of AI remains one of the most informed and intelligent critiques of AI as it developed in the '70s.
Searle's Chinese Room thought experiment challenges the claims of 'strong' AI.
Starting with Chapter 8, Mind Design II shows clear signs of the editor's decision to place heavy emphasis on the connectionist approach.
Churchland surveys the problems afflicting the classical approach to understanding cognition.
Mind Design II is a unique contribution that argues against both Fodor and Pylyshyn.
The book concludes with a bold attempt to establish a research approach different from traditional computational approaches.
There are 22 pages of references in Mind Design II compared to 14 pages in Mind Design.

These words of Peter Aaron as he sits down to tell the story of his best friend, Benjamin Sachs, in Paul Auster's brilliant novel Leviathan strike me as a good description of what one feels upon reading this important collection of papers by John McCarthy.

Since the dawn of theoretical computer science, McCarthy has been a fertile source of bright ideas and, like so many other people in the field of artificial intelligence (AI), I have been stimulated by his thinking.
However, when I reflect on the primary quality that draws me to his work, I realize that one aspect that stands out among others is the beauty of his prose.
What one immediately notices in reading this collection of papers are those very special literary abilities of McCarthy, which are equaled, in my view, only by Marvin Minsky.
A major feature of McCarthy's prose is the freshness of his style.
His witty and striking examples give great vitality to his presentations which are clearly marked by an absence of confusion and disorder.
True, McCarthy has his uncertainties, but these are really of a different order - difficulties that are bred by the tough problems that he invariably grapples with.
Seventeen papers written by McCarthy on the subject of common sense are collected here.
We learn from Minsky that McCarthy's general program to formalize common sense took shape almost 35 years ago.
Chapter 2 presents in detail how McCarthy went about to accomplish this goal.
The advice taker is the proposed program for common-sense reasoning.

McCarthy gives the following working definition: a program has common sense if it automatically deduces for itself a sufficiently wide class of immediate consequences of anything it is told and what it already knows.
The advice taker system has the following main features: There is a method of representing expressions in the computer.
Certain of these expressions are declarative sentences in a logical system.
There is a deduction routine which when presented a set of premises will deduce a set of immediate conclusions.
The intelligence of advice taker is not embodied in this deduction routine; rather, it is embodied in the procedures which choose the input to the deduction routine.
Each object has a property list which includes the specific things one would like to say about it.
The program operates by cyclically applying the deduction routine to a list of premises and by obeying some of the conclusions that have the form of imperative sentences.
Chapter 3 studies some of the problems of philosophy which arise in any serious discussion of a program such as the advice taker.
It is a rich paper which touches on a wide range of issues and cannot be done justice in the space available to this review.
The situation calculus is introduced, and the frame problem is stated in stunning clarity.
This is a computational epistemology paper.
More specifically, we want a program such as the advice taker to decide what to do by deducing in a formal language that a certain approach will lead it to its goal.
Philosophically speaking, this would amount to formalizing the concepts of causality, ability, intention, and above all knowledge.
Two papers in this collection belong to the interface between common-sense reasoning and natural language semantics.
Chapter 5 quotes a newspaper story describing a rather outlandish adventure of a certain Mr. Hug in a freight elevator.
Before a program is declared to have digested the story of Mr. Hug, it would have to be able to answer a bunch of questions that cover important aspects of the story.
McCarthy makes up such a list in order to get some intuitive idea of what common-sense skills are involved in penetrating the surface composition of the given narrative.

A long time ago, Voltaire wrote that sens commun (common sense) means good sense, crude reason, the beginnings of reason, the first notion of ordinary things, a state midway between stupidity and intelligence.
Today, thanks to McCarthy, we are able to form a much more refined view of this popular phrase.

Unlike Forguson's very readable but nontechnical monograph, the theory of common sense, as developed by McCarthy and cast into this volume by Lifschitz, oftentimes includes beautiful mathematical constructions and difficult results.
Researchers interested in building common-sense theories should read this book in order to comprehend the fascinating world of common-sense reasoning.
Set theory is a branch of modern mathematics with a unique place because various other branches can be formally defined within it.
For example, Book I of the influential works of N. Bourbaki is devoted to the theory of sets and provides the framework for the remaining volumes.

Bourbaki said in 1949: '[A]ll mathematical theories may be regarded as extensions of the general theory of sets . . . [O]n these foundations I can state that I can build up the whole of the mathematics of the present day.'
This brings up the possibility of using set theory in foundational studies in AI.
McCarthy has emphasized the need for fundamental research in AI and claimed that AI needs mathematical and logical theory involving conceptual innovations.

In an opening address, he stressed the feasibility of using set theory in AI because there is considerable beauty, economy, and naturalness in using sets for information modeling and knowledge representation.
In this paper, we first give a brief review of 'classical' set theory.
We avoid the technical details and instead focus on the underlying concepts.

While we assume little or no technical background in set theory per se, we hope that the reader is interested in the applications of this formal theory to the problems of intelligent information management.
We then consider the alternative set theories which have been proposed to overcome the limitations of the standard theory.
Finally, we survey various 'nonstandard' treatments of set theory, each innovating different aspects such as urelements, cumulative hierarchy, self-reference, cardinality, well-orderings, and so on.
G. Cantor's work on the theory of infinite series should be considered as the foundation of the research in set theory.
In Cantor's conception, a set is a collection into a whole of definite, distinct objects of our perception or our thought (the elements of the set).
This property of definiteness implies that given a set and an object, it is possible to determine if the object is a member of that set.
In other words, a set is completely determined by its members.
In the initial stages of his research, Cantor did not work from axioms.

However, all of his theorems can be derived from three axioms: Extensionality which states that two sets are identical if they have the same members, Abstraction which states that for any given property there is a set whose members are just those entities having that property, and Choice which states that if b is a set, all of whose elements are nonempty sets no two of which have any elements in common, then there is a set c which has precisely one element in common with each element of b.
The theory was soon threatened by the introduction of some paradoxes which led to its evolution.
In 1902, B. Russell found a contradiction in G. Frege's foundational system which was developed on Cantor's naive conception.
This contradiction could be derived from the Axiom of Abstraction by considering 'the set of all things which have the property of not being members of themselves.'
Another antinomy occurred with the 'set of all sets.'
The well-known Cantor's Theorem states that the power set of V has a greater cardinality than V itself.
This is paradoxical since V by definition is the most inclusive set.
This is the so-called Cantor's Paradox and led to discussions on the size of comprehensible sets.
The new axiomatizations took a common step for overcoming the deficiencies of the naive approach by introducing classes.
NBG, which was proposed by von Neumann and later revised and simplified by P. Bernays and Godel, was the most popular of these.
In NBG, there are three primitive notions: set, class, and membership.
Classes are considered as totalities corresponding to some, but not necessarily all, properties.
The classical paradoxes are avoided by recognizing two types of classes: sets and proper classes.
A class is a set if it is a member of some class.
Otherwise, it is a proper class.
Russell's Paradox is avoided by showing that the class Y = {x : x ~ x} is a proper class, not a set.
The axioms of NBG are simply chosen with respect to the limitation of size constraint.
If we want to design artificial systems which will work in the real world, they must have a good knowledge of that world and be able to make inferences out of their knowledge.
The common knowledge which is possessed by any child and the methods of making inferences from this knowledge are known as common sense.
Any intelligent task requires it to some degree and designing programs with common sense is one of the most important problems in AI.

McCarthy claims that the first task in the construction of a general intelligent program is to define a naive commonsense view of the world precisely enough, but also adds that this is a very difficult thing.
He states that 'a program has common sense if it automatically deduces for itself a sufficiently wide class of immediate consequences of anything it is told and what it already knows.'
It appears that in commonsense reasoning a concept can be considered as an indivisible unit, or as composed of other parts, as in mathematics.
Relationships, again as in mathematics, can also be represented with sets.
Cowen showed, in a landmark paper, that researchers in both set theory and computer science are studying similar objects: graphs, conjunctive normal forms, set systems, etc. and their interrelations.
The moral is that advances in one area can then often be of use in the other.
Gilmore provides evidence, within the framework of his NaDSet theory, that the absolute character of ZF or NBG set theories is not easy to support.
Set theory has also been the subject of research in automated theorem proving.
Brown gave a deductive system for elementary set theory which is based on truth-value preserving transformations.
Quaife presented a new clausal version of NBG, comparing it with the one given in Boyer et al. and claimed that automated development of set theory could be improved.
Set theory can be useful in intelligent information management.
The methodology may change, of course.
A universal set theory, answering many technical questions in information management, can be developed by means of proposing new axioms or modifying existing ones.
Alternatively and more conservatively, different set-theoretic concepts may be examined and modified based on existing set theories.
No matter what proposal is followed, we believe that further research in this field should be to the advantage of the IIS community.
In human communication using natural language, there is potential for a certain intricacy regarding the communicative mode and 'what is said'.

The following anecdote illustrates this point: Once upon a time, Stalin read out in public a telegram from Trotsky: 'You were right and I was wrong. You are the true heir of Lenin. I should apologize.'
A Jewish tailor then stepped from the crowd and explained to Stalin how he ought to have read the message: 'You were right and I was wrong? You are the true heir of Lenin? I should apologize???!!'
While one appreciates the crucial role of intonation in this story, it is the historical background through which the intended meaning is contextually determined.
Thus, Stalin's rendering of the individual words or phrases makes sense, but it is the 'deconstructive' reading of the tailor that shows the determinate meaning of Trotsky's message.
But, how does one really purport to know the intended meaning of a given message?
Few would deny that in the process of construing meaning, one is caught in the act of contextualizing—placing things in context.
In studying this act in detail, it is unavoidable to notice the interaction of authorial intentions and context.
Strawson's recent volume of essays, Entity and Identity, addresses this very question.
In these essays, Strawson advances a threefold distinction regarding how context bears on the meaning of 'what is said' when a sentence is uttered.
Strawson tackles the riddle of how context influences intended meaning by proposing a simple question and an economic answer.
Assume that a certain sentence S of a language L was seriously uttered on some occasion.
Let us grant that the hearer possesses full mastery of the syntax and semantics of L.
The question is whether the hearer can know the meaning of precisely what was said on that occasion.
Strawson's proposed scheme consists of three progressively richer senses of meaning: sense-A-meaning, sense-B-meaning, and sense-C-meaning.
Sense-A-meaning is linguistic meaning.
Suppose S is free of ambiguity, or X is informed which of the alternative readings of S is the right one.
We say that X knows the sense-A-meaning of 'what is said'.
An important characteristic of such meaning is that if X has access to it, then X can give a correct translation of S into another language.
For example, if S is 'The collapse of the bank took everyone by surprise,' once the intended designation is clarified, the translation proceeds smoothly.
Sense-B-meaning is linguistic-cum-referential meaning.
X learns the sense-B-meaning of S if he has access to the references of proper names or indexicals contained in S.
For instance, if S is 'He stood on his head since then,' and X learns the reference of 'he' and 'then', then X knows a richer meaning.
Sense-C-meaning is the complete meaning of a message.
It is obtained by adding to sense-B-meaning the illocutionary force of what was said, along with a complete grasp of how what was said is intended to be understood.
For instance, if S is 'Don't sign that contract yet,' X needs to know whether this was issued as a request, a command, or advice.
Strawson explores the specific differences in how the meaning of 'what is said' depends on context in the three cases.
Context influences sense-A-meaning in situations where S suffers from syntactic and/or lexical ambiguity.
Disambiguation of S by context is not generally a matter of linguistic rule but rather of general relevance.
Strawson notes several points where his threefold distinction is too crude to account for all complexities of language use.
He discusses semantic creativity, the seriousness of utterances, and the nuances of reference.
He also addresses the challenges of translation and the implications of radical interpretation.
The originator of a message assumes background knowledge on the part of the addressee.
The task of the addressee is to narrow down the list of meanings available and attain the intended meaning.
By enveloping the message in increasingly narrower contexts, the number of meanings is reduced, ideally isolating just one meaning.

When I finished reading this book, I was reminded of the opening stanza of Spirit Song Over the Waters, a poem by Johann Wolfgang Goethe: The soul of man resembleth water: From heaven it cometh, To heaven it soareth, And then again To earth descendeth, Changing ever.

I now think that McDermott's closing lines were instrumental in elevating my spirits: We must look for a coherent synthesis of our religious intuitions and scientific discoveries, so that as the very definition of what it is to be human changes, we will have a hope that our moral intuitions will not degenerate; or if not a hope, at least a prayer.
What is Mind and Mechanism about? Despite the experience I have just related, this book is not about ethical or religious affairs.
A well-known AI researcher, McDermott is interested in computational approaches to consciousness.
His reason for working in the field of AI is to solve the mind-body problem.
In other words, his long-range goal is to understand how a physical organ, viz. the brain, can have experiences.
This is a tough project because it involves the elucidation of the relationship between our mentality and the physical foundation of our body.
How can a biological/chemical system (i.e., the human body) have beliefs, desires, intentions, and so on?
Physicists have persuasive reasons to make us believe that ours is a material world that obeys physical laws.
Once we commit ourselves to this view, it sounds quite bewildering-even enigmatic-to think that there is a place for independently existing minds in such a world.
When physicists speak, McDermott listens.
As he makes clear on the first page of Chapter 1, his hypothesis is that we are all contraptions designed by evolution.
The concept of mind arises because people's brains are biological computers.
Crudely put, minds are produced by computers.

The book consists of the following chapters: 1. The Problem of Phenomenal Consciousness, 2. Artificial Intelligence, 3. A Computational Theory of Consciousness, 4. Objections and Replies, 5. Symbols and Semantics, 6. Consequences.
Chapter 2, the longest, is a masterly account of the state of the art in AI.

Discussed in this chapter are computational mechanisms for such classical problems of AI as game-playing, neural networks, computer vision, robotics, speech-recognition/language-understanding, and automated theorem-proving.
McDermott sees mind as a self-fulfilling description, a description that brings mind into being.
He offers a fine analogy by considering the windows in the user interface of a personal computer.
These windows are there because the computer is working in a way supporting their existence.
In a nutshell, a formal description starts to act causatively when interpreted by a computer.
For McDermott, the problem of phenomenal consciousness-how a physical object can have experiences-is the toughest nut to crack.
To put the matter differently, explaining what it is to have qualia is the hardest problem.
McDermott first tries to demystify the notion of free will.
His insight is that a robot must model itself in a different way from other objects in its world in order to avoid infinite regress.
Chapter 4 is devoted to a thorough defense of these proposals against various objections.
Discussed in Chapter 5 are numerous full-fledged or partial theories of consciousness or related matters by influential philosophers.
Almost all of McDermott's arguments and analyses in this chapter are to the point, upright, and illuminating.
Assume we build a robot which is just like an average person when it comes to attributes such as love, morality, aesthetics, humor, etc.
Now, it is conceivable that by just tweaking some program variables, we could get radically different versions of these attributes.
McDermott states that a robot can have phenomenal consciousness but lack morals.
The last big question that McDermott grapples with is belief in God in the absence of dualist nonphysical realms.
His stance is not antireligionist; he doesn't think that religion is a menacing force.
McDermott is convinced that mankind will always be troubled by finiteness and long for the comfort provided by the unfathomable or incomprehensible.
One strength of this book is its almost encyclopedic coverage.
McDermott has this natural gift for explaining the knotty or perplexing with such grace and vividness that one cannot help but admire his virtuosity.
If you want an intuitive grasp of what is keeping philosophers of mind busy nowadays read this book.
Context has emerged as a central concept in a variety of contemporary approaches to reasoning.

The conference at which the papers in this volume were presented was the third international, interdisciplinary conference on the topic of context, and was held in Dundee, Scotland on July 27-30, 2001.
The first conference in this series was held in Rio de Janeiro in 1997, and the second in Trento in 1999.

Like the previous conferences, CONTEXT 2001 was remarkably successful in bringing together representatives of many different fields, spanning the entire range of the cognitive and informational sciences, and with interests ranging from specific, commercial applications to highly general philosophical and logical theories.
The papers collected here demonstrate well the range of context-related research.

While foundational problems remain, and continue to be discussed in many of the contributions collected in this volume, the work shows increased sophistication about what forms of reasoning are important, and what techniques are appropriate in accounting for them.

The papers themselves, however, do not convey the lively excitement of the conference itself, and the continuing spirit of cooperation and communication across disciplines that has been the hallmark of these conferences.
We are very pleased that the field of context research has shown over four years intense, sustained development while retaining this sense of interdisciplinary cooperation.

Serious thinking about the computational aspects of situation theory has started only a decade ago.
There have been recent proposals in this direction, with varying degrees of divergence from the ontology of the theory.
We believe that a programming environment incorporating bona fide situation-theoretic constructs will be useful in AI and describe our very recent BABY-SIT implementation.
A brief account of PROSIT and ASTL is also offered in order to put BABY-SIT into perspective.
While BABY-SIT is a general-purpose programming environment, in this paper we demonstrate its operation on a well-known example from the AI literature, viz. the Yale Shooting Problem (YSP).

Since our essential aim is to display the available functionalities of BABY-SIT for representational issues in AI, we simply borrow a theoretical approach – causal theories due to Yoav Shoham – to solve the YSP.
It should be noted that our goal in writing this paper is not to offer a new approach to formal temporal reasoning.
There are numerous works in AI to that effect.
Neither do we want our work to be understood as a temporal data (world model) manager.
Situation theory is a unified mathematical theory of information content.
The original proposal was due to Jon Barwise and John Perry.
The theory has matured over the last decade or so and various versions of it have been applied to a number of problems in logic, language, and cognition.
In this section, we introduce the basic notions of situation theory.
The basic ontology of situation theory consists of entities that a finite cognitive agent individuates and/or discriminates as it makes its way in the world.
These entities are known as uniformities and include individuals, relations, spatial locations, temporal locations, situations, and types.
A scheme of individuation is an essential aspect of situation theory.
In situation theory, information is always taken to be information about some situation and is in the form of discrete items.
Infons are these discrete items of information and situations are first-class objects which describe limited portions of the real world.
Two pioneering systems, PROSIT and ASTL, incorporate only some of the original features of situation theory; the remaining features they omit for the sake of achieving particular goals.
In BABY-SIT, we have tried to stick to the essentials of the theory and adopted the ontology which was first put forward by Barwise and Perry, and then refined by Devlin.
PROSIT (PROgramming in SItuation Theory) was developed by Nakashima et al. and implemented in Lisp.
In PROSIT one can define situations and assert knowledge into particular situations.
It is also possible to define relations between situations in the form of constraints.
There is an inference engine similar to a Prolog interpreter.
One can assert facts that a situation will support.
ASTL (A Situation Theoretic Language) is another programming language based on situation theory.
One can define in ASTL constraints and rules of inference over the situations.
BABY-SIT has been developed in KEE (Knowledge Engineering Environment).

The primary motivation underlying BABY-SIT is to facilitate the development and testing of programs in domains ranging from linguistics to AI within a unified framework built upon situation-theoretic constructs.
BABY-SIT accommodates the basic features of situation theory and enhances these features compared to the existing approaches.
There are nine basic types which are employed in BABY-SIT: individuals, times, places, relations, polarities, infons, parameters, situations, and types.
In BABY-SIT, situations are viewed at an abstract level.
This means that situations are sets of parametric infons, but they may be non-well-founded (circular).
All situations are required to cohere.
Relations are categorized into two: infonic relations that can be used as major constituents of infons, and non-infonic relations that can only fill the argument roles of infonic relations.

A loaded gun, after waiting for a while, is fired at Fred.
What are the results of this action?

Strawson proposed in the early seventies an attractive threefold distinction regarding how context bears on the meaning of 'what is said' when a sentence is uttered.
The proposed scheme is somewhat crude and, being aware of this aspect, Strawson himself raised various points to make it more adequate.
In this paper, we review the scheme of Strawson, note his concerns, and add some of our own.
However, our main point is to defend the essence of Strawson's approach and to recommend it as a starting point for research into intended meaning and context.

Strawson tackles the riddle of how context influences intended meaning by first proposing a simple question and an economic answer, and then attending to the complications which seem not to be easily resolvable by the latter.
Assume that a certain sentence S of a language L (e.g. English) was seriously uttered on some occasion.
The question is: Is there any sense in which X can be said to know the meaning of precisely what was said on the occasion in question?
Strawson's proposed scheme to investigate this problem consists of three progressively richer senses of meaning which he dubs sense-A-meaning, sense-B-meaning, and sense-C-meaning.
Strawson's distinction is a natural one.
To support this premise, another threefold distinction due to Leech is worth indicating at this point.
Leech states that specification of context has the effect of narrowing down the communicative possibilities of a message.

In particularizing meaning, context helps in eliminating certain ambiguities, indicating the referents of certain types of words, and supplying information which the speaker/writer has omitted through ellipsis.

Having defined the three senses of meaning, Strawson turns to the question of what specific differences are there in the ways in which the meaning of 'what is said' depends on context in the three cases.
Context bears on determination of sense-A-meaning in situations where S suffers from syntactic and/or lexical ambiguity.
Disambiguation of S by context at this level is not in general a matter of linguistic rule or convention.
Context bears on the determination of sense-B-meaning in all cases except those where B-knowledge adds nothing to A-knowledge.
Strawson enumerated several points at which his threefold distinction is too crude to provide for all the complexities of language use.
One issue is semantic creativity, where meanings of a particular word may not be listed priorly in X's ideal lexicon.
Another issue is the seriousness of utterances; ironical utterances cannot be easily dismissed as aberrations.
Strawson notes that a declarative sentence uttered ironically may express an idea that contradicts the idea which it professes to express.
The following are not so much weaknesses of Strawson's scheme as possible avenues of research for streamlining it.
One point is radical interpretation, where if A-knowledge is null, X cannot even study the question properly.
Another point is the use of context to figure out which language is being spoken.
Contextual domains refer to the implicit restrictions of natural language quantifiers.
The originator of a message usually assumes quite a bit of background knowledge on the part of an addressee.
The task of the addressee is to narrow down the list of meanings available to him and attain the intended meaning.
By 'enveloping' it in increasingly narrower contexts, the number of meanings is reduced.
This paper argued that there is a persuasive approach to studying the feasibility of this problem, first spelled out in earlier works by Strawson.

The importance of contextual reasoning is emphasized by various researchers in AI.
Here, we survey the problem of formalizing context and explore what is needed for an acceptable account of this abstract notion.
The issue of context arises in various areas of AI, including knowledge representation, natural language processing, and intelligent information retrieval.
Although the word context is frequently used in descriptions, explanations, and analyses of computer programs in these areas, its meaning is frequently left to the reader's understanding.
Context is a crucial factor in communication.
Ordinary observation proves its importance: Just consider the confusion that results from the lack of contextual information when, for example, you join a scheduled meeting half an hour late.
Without the clues of the original context, you might find it hard to make sense of the ongoing discussion.
Participants would realize that they cannot assume a lot about your background knowledge and give you a quick rundown of the conversations so far.
Clark and Carlson regard context as information that is available to a person for interaction with a particular process on a given occasion.
The intrinsic context for grasping what a speaker means on some occasion is the totality of the knowledge, beliefs, and suppositions that are shared by the speaker and the listener.
Leech gives another particularly attractive quasi-definition, stating that the specification of context has the effect of narrowing down the communicative possibilities of the message.

According to the Oxford English Dictionary, the term context typically has two primary meanings: the words around a word, phrase, statement, and the general conditions in which an event, action, takes place.
The first definition is closely related to linguistic meaning, whereas the second is closer to a desirable account of context in AI.
Categorization is one of the basic mental processes in cognition.
We can categorize various types of objects, events, and states of affairs, and our categorizations depend on the circumstance and perspective.
Barwise and Seligman use natural regularities to study the role of context in categorization.
A formal notion of context might be useful in information retrieval because it can increase performance by providing a framework for well-defined queries and intelligent text matching.
Given the explicit context, a query might be better described, enhancing recall and precision.
When we state something, we do so in a context.
If we are to reason in a commonsense way, we have to use certain contexts.
The importance of the notion of context has been realized by philosophers for centuries.
The notion of context was first introduced to AI in a logicist framework by McCarthy.
McCarthy states three reasons for introducing the formal notion of context.
The use of context allows simple axiomatizations and enables the use of a specific vocabulary of information about a circumstance.
The idea of formalizing context seems to have caught on and produced good theoretical outcomes.
However, the area of innovative applications remains relatively unexplored, where further research on context should converge.
Context is a criterion in settling the question of why a man who has just put a cigarette in his mouth has put his hand in his pocket.

As with other widely used notions that are commonly referred to in everyday activities without much hesitation, context is difficult to analyze scientifically and grasp in all its different demeanors.
In our routine communicative activities, context is exploited both in production and in comprehension, and is strictly related to another problematic notion, viz. meaning.
Without context, words and actions have no meaning at all. This is true not only of human communication in words but also of all communication whatsoever, of all mental process, of all mind.

The notion of context has gained significance, and is more often resorted to not only in disciplines where it has always played a central role but also in other disciplines, such as history or biology.

Nowadays in every research domain—AI, psychology, neurosciences, anthropology, economics, aesthetics, sociology, etc.—the word 'context' is repeatedly mentioned, though its relevance and its significance with regard to the given discipline are rarely made explicit.
Human beings are very good at using context without thinking about it.
However, problems arise when one tries to model an average behavior or when one tries to cope with a different cultural context that asks for different behaviors.
There are so many different ways of using the term 'context' that it would be better to speak of a 'family-resemblance' concept.
The notion of context is a complex one, and several components should—and have been—focused upon over the years by scholars in various theoretical frameworks.
If we adopt a prototype model, we could better individuate two points of attraction around which the various notions of context seem to converge: a local point and a global point.
A local notion of context has recently gained the upper hand especially in the conversationalist approach, where its flexibility and its resilience have been repeatedly stressed.

Accordingly, instead of a general updated overview of the use of context in every conceivable specific field, we will offer the readers of this special issue an introduction to the problems involved in the study of context by way of eight papers encompassing eight different areas.
The problems encountered with context are in general insoluble.
This notion lays an intellectual burden on us that, while remaining inescapable, can become so heavy that it destroys the understanding it was created to further.
We hope that the papers in this special issue help contribute towards a better understanding of context and thus towards a less pessimistic outlook vis-à-vis this key concept.

Our long-term goal is to offer a full-fledged formalization of context, one that can be used in, among other areas, natural language processing.

In this paper, which can be regarded as a tentative step toward that end, we will identify the role of context in language and take a look at some salient efforts in (logical) AI treating formal contexts.
In general, the focus of our discussion will be McCarthy's proposal, which is the groundwork for all ensuing logicist formalizations.

While the main purpose of McCarthy, viz. a mechanism by which we can build AI systems which are not forever stuck with the concepts they use at a given time, is still largely unfulfilled, we will see that important advances have been made.
Our model of context, on the other hand, is inspired by the pioneering work of Barwise on conditionals, and will be presented using the notation and terminology of situation theory.

After giving the minimum background to situation theory, we will state this model and discuss an application of it in lifting, i.e., the process of computing what is true in one context based on what is true in another context.
The situation theoretic model has notable properties such as partiality, dynamic contexts, and natural language support.
'You shall know a word by the company it keeps.' This remark of J. R. Firth seems to us an apt reminder for the ubiquity of context.
According to Crystal, 'context' is a general term in linguistics and phonetics to refer to specific parts of an utterance (or text) near or adjacent to a unit which is the focus of attention.
The occurrence of a unit is partly or wholly determined by its context, which is specified in terms of the unit's relations.
Blackburn offers a similar definition: 'In linguistics, context is the parts of an utterance surrounding a unit and which may affect both its meaning and its grammatical contribution.'
However, he is quick to add that context also refers to 'the wider situation, either of the speaker or of the surroundings, that may play a part in determining the significance of a saying.'
Leech notes that the specification of context has the effect of narrowing down the communicative possibilities of a message.

This particularization of meaning can take place in assorted ways, including: (i) elimination of certain ambiguities or multiple meanings in the message, (ii) clarification of the referents of deictics and definite descriptions, (iii) supplying of information which the writer has omitted through ellipsis, (iv) interpretation of tense, and (v) determination of the scope of quantifiers.
It is standard nowadays to use the term 'co-text' for the narrow, purely linguistic context.

He believes that natural language meaning must be studied as a multiple phenomenon, its numerous aspects being relatable to different levels of linguistic analysis and features of the world.

Being one of those linguistic abstractions that is constantly used in all kinds of contexts but never explained, the establishment of relevant context in NLP is traditionally seen as a formidable problem.
Roughly speaking, 'context' can be the whole world in relation to an utterance act.
However, observations show that the quest for idealized, context-independent meaning is seriously misdirected.
Taking an engineering attitude and studying contexts as mathematical entities with properties useful in AI or NLP seems to be the only viable approach.
McCarthy offers no definition of context.
His underlying assumption is that 'there are mathematical context structures of different properties, some of which are useful.'
McCarthy's basic relation relating contexts and propositions is that proposition p is true in context c.
The origin of this relation can be traced to the Turing lecture of McCarthy.
McCarthy notes that formulas are always considered as themselves asserted within an outer context.

The importance of this for NLP can be seen by noticing that although the set of propositions true in a context may be finite, the collection of natural language sentences that can express these propositions will be infinite.
Contexts are 'first-class citizens.'
We can use contexts in our logical formulas in the same way we use other objects.
In other words, contexts are formal objects in the semantics; they can be denoted by constants in the logical language and when necessary, variables can range over them.
Each context has a vocabulary associated with it.
Thus, a given statement may not be expressible in some context due to the impoverished vocabulary of that context.
It is noted that since there is no absolute outermost context, it is necessary to have an adequate notion of transcendence.
Transcendence is the way to relax or modify some assumptions of an old context.
In order to implement transcendence, an appropriate set of nonmonotonic rules for lifting sentences to broader contexts is required.
Situation theory is a mathematical theory of information.
Two of its primitive concepts are infons and situations.
Infons are the basic units that embody discrete items of information.
A situation is a limited portion of the world, which can be picked out by a cognitive agent.
It thus corresponds rather well to the intuitive meaning of 'situation' in English.
For example, the sentence 'I solved a puzzle during the invited talk of Cooper' describes an activity performed at a particular time and location.
Using a notation hinting at first-order logic, a situation is said to support an infon provided that the infon is true of situations.
Abstract situations are the mathematical counterparts of real situations, and unlike the latter, are amenable to symbolic manipulation.
Let s be a given situation.
Following the standard practice, we require the availability of some device for making reference to arbitrary objects of a given type, namely parameters.
In situation theory, the flow of information is realized via constraints.
We denote a constraint as S1 ⇒ S2, where S1 and S2 are situation types.
Cognitively, if this relation holds, then it is a fact that if S1 is realized, then so is S2.
Lifting axioms are used to relate truth in one context to truth in another context.
Since the vocabularies, languages, and assumptions of the source context and target context are usually different, these differences need to be addressed during the lifting.
Lifting needs to be as 'meaning-preserving' as possible and this makes it useful for NLP applications where preserving meaning is highly desirable.
Consider the following simple scenario which shows that a person interested in NLP should care about lifting: Fred is standing in front of Chris.
There is a flower pot to the left of Chris.
Fred says 'I like that flower pot to your left.'
Let this statement be F1 and the context in which this is uttered be C1.
Chris then moves so that the flower pot is to his right and tells Fred that he did not hear what Fred just said and asks him to say it again.
Fred wants to convey the same message in this new context but cannot use the same sentence.
The sentence which states the same thing in this new context is 'I like that flower pot to your right.'
Call this second sentence F2.
F1 states in C1 exactly what F2 states in C2.
Given F1, C1, and C2, the process of obtaining F2 from F1 is called lifting F1 from C1 to C2.
