They excel in domains where human experts possess specialized knowledge and experience that can be codified into a set of rules or algorithms.
Expert systems have found applications in various fields, including medicine, finance, engineering, and manufacturing.
The key advantage of expert systems lies in their ability to provide consistent, reliable, and efficient decision-making processes, even in the absence of human experts.
They can analyze large amounts of data, evaluate multiple options, and generate recommendations based on predefined rules and logical reasoning.

They rely on the accuracy and completeness of the knowledge base and may struggle with new or unfamiliar situations that fall outside their predefined rules.
Additionally, maintaining and updating the knowledge base can be challenging, requiring ongoing collaboration with domain experts to ensure its relevance and accuracy.

We propose to characterize imaginative resistance as the failure or unwillingness of the reader to take a fictional description of a deviant reality at face value.
The goal of the paper is to explore how readers deal with such a breakdown of the default Face Value interpretation strategy.
We posit two distinct interpretative 'coping' strategies which help the reader engage with the resistance-inducing fiction by attributing the offending content to one of the fictional characters.
Consider the following mini-fiction: Sara never liked animals. One day, her father caught her kicking the neighbor's dog.
When we get to the final sentence our engagement with the fiction falters.
Some philosophers of art have sought to explain when and why the reader's imaginative engagement and/or the author's authority to create fictional truths of their choosing breaks down here.
This paper adopts the position that imaginative resistance is merely the breakdown of a default interpretation strategy, which we call 'Face Value'.

Applying Face Value to the mini-fiction amounts to taking the text as presenting us with a fictional world where killing the fish would, in fact, be the right thing to do in the circumstances described.
In this section we explore how readers interpret various types of stories that philosophers have devised to elicit imaginative resistance.
The Face Value strategy involves taking the text as an accurate description of a fictional world.
The Character Perspective strategy involves viewing a certain passage as involving a shift to the perspective of one of the salient characters.
The Narrator Accommodation strategy involves inferring a personal narrator and interpreting the relevant passage as a description of their unreliable mental state.
In the following sections, we propose a uniform SDRT implementation of the main coping mechanisms we hypothesized above.
We start by showing how fiction could be interpreted in DRT, a general representational framework for analyzing discourse meaning beyond the individual sentence level.
We add some basic tools from SDRT, an extension of DRT that takes discourse coherence as a guiding principle of interpretation.
Some stories are hard to take at face value.
This paper doesn't directly contribute to debates about imaginative resistance.
Instead, we take imaginative resistance to be the breakdown of a default interpretation strategy, Face Value, and explore possible other, equally valid and indeed common interpretation mechanisms.

One key feature of both our present age and the decades to come is that we face the increasing arrival of powerful AI in many important domains of our lives.
Many authors have argued that this raises new and deep ethical challenges.
One of the philosophically most interesting is, as Christian List has recently put it, that we may have to adjust some of our conventional anthropocentric approaches to morality.
The arrival of powerful AI suggests that our moral theories and regulatory frameworks should be 'future-proofed', i.e., reassessed in the face of these developments.
One core part of our regulatory frameworks that can be found almost universally across human societies are our practices of praise and blame.
Praising others for commendable behavior and blaming them for transgressions is one of the key forms that our regulatory interactions can take.

Hence, one important part of future-proofing our extant regulatory frameworks in the face of the increasing arrival of powerful AI is to ask whether it makes sense to extend these practices and, in particular, our practice of blame to these systems.
Our main claim is that, contrary to what one might initially think, this question should be answered in the affirmative.
We shall argue that it can make sense to blame AI systems.
More specifically, we shall defend the claim that we have a pro tanto reason to extend our blaming practices to these systems.
The claim that the increasing arrival of AI gives rise to deep ethical challenges is a commonplace.

Things become more interesting, though, once we ask why exactly the ethical challenges raised by AI systems seem to be of a more fundamental nature than the challenges raised by the increasing reliance on traditional machines since the Industrial Revolution.

Unlike the machines that arrived during the Industrial Revolution, we now face systems that have the ability to operate relatively autonomously in largely uncontrolled environments and make high-stakes decisions.
If an AI system operates relatively freely in a largely uncontrolled environment, or if it can make high-stakes decisions on its own, then the societal implications are qualitatively novel.
We are then dealing with artefacts as genuine decision-makers, perhaps for the first time in human history.

If the development of novel AI systems were restricted to sophisticated vending machines or systems that can autonomously assemble furniture, few would feel that the ethical challenges these systems raise were qualitatively novel.
However, the development of AI systems includes entities like driverless cars, autonomous air vehicles, and medical helper AI systems, which operate in high-stakes contexts.
Due to their increasingly autonomous mode of functioning, it will be increasingly difficult to hold some human being responsible for that harm.
All of this suggests that our moral theories and regulatory frameworks should be 'future-proofed', i.e., reassessed in the face of these developments.
To a first approximation, blame can be characterized as a reaction to something of negative normative significance about someone or their behavior.
Together with many theorists working on blame, we shall assume that manifestations of blame can be quite diverse.
Among other things, they can take the form of openly expressed anger, unexpressed feelings of resentment, or even seemingly dispassionate acts of relationship-modification.
To settle the issue of whether it makes sense to extend our blaming practices to AI systems, we propose that the best answer is to focus on blame's functions.

Our suggestion relies on two background assumptions: (1) Our blaming practices fulfill several valuable functions, and (2) If our blaming practices would still fulfill their valuable functions in targeting entities of type x, then we have a pro tanto reason to extend these practices to entities of type x.
One valuable function of our blaming practices is retribution, which helps ensure that the guilty get what they deserve.
However, we are skeptical about this function when targeting AI systems, as it is difficult to see how blaming responses could be harmful to them.
Another important function of blame is to modify the future behavior of the blamee.
In order for blame to fulfill its behavior-modification function when targeting an AI system, the latter would need to possess some kind of feedback mechanism.
We argue that there do not seem to be any in-principle obstacles to AI systems being able to learn from blame.
Blame also serves the function of initiating or sustaining conversations about the negative normative or evaluative status of what happened.
Even if we cannot converse with a self-driving car, we can converse with each other about the normative status of its actions.
Another important function of blame is to enable a specific form of moral protest, which can be fulfilled even if the blamee is an AI system.
Blame also signals one's commitment to certain norms and values, which can be important in social contexts.
Finally, blame can help manage relationships, allowing us to revise our attitudes towards entities that fail to meet our expectations.
To show that it can be fully appropriate to blame AI systems, one would also have to show that AI systems can be morally responsible agents.
List suggests that certain forms of holding responsible other than blame should be extended to AI systems.
Assuming List's optimistic stance is correct, we have reason to assume that it will be fully appropriate to extend our blaming practices to some future AI systems.
However, not everyone will share this optimistic stance.
If there are in-principle obstacles to AI systems fulfilling the conditions for blameworthiness, it may seem that our reasoning would be of merely theoretical interest.
However, one key motive for avoiding 'blame without blameworthiness' no longer seems to apply when the blamee is an AI system.
This enables us to arrive at the conclusion that we might still have good reason to extend our blaming practices to these systems.
A common and important part of our everyday moral lives is to blame ourselves and others for bad conduct.
The arrival of powerful AI systems that operate autonomously in high-stakes contexts raises the question of whether it makes sense to target these systems with blame.

We have argued for the claim that it indeed makes sense to include these systems in our blaming practices, since many of the important functions that are fulfilled by blaming humans can also be served by blaming AI systems.
This gives us good pro tanto reason to extend our blaming practices to AI systems.

Our ConvNet will be a stack of alternated Conv2D (with ReLU activation) and MaxPooling2D layers.
Since we are dealing with bigger images and a more complex problem, we will make our network larger with one more Conv2D + MaxPooling2D stage.
This serves both to augment the capacity of the network and to further reduce the size of the feature maps.
We end up with feature maps of size 7x7 right before the Flatten layer.
The depth of the feature maps increases in the network while the size decreases.
Since we are tackling a multi-classification problem, we end the network with a single unit (a Dense layer of size 1) and a sigmoid activation.
This unit encodes the probability that the network is looking at one class or the other.
For our compilation step, we'll use the RMSprop optimizer and categorical crossentropy as our loss.
We conducted experiments with the ConvNet from scratch using the lemons image dataset that consists of 2000 images after resizing them to 150x150 pixels.
We divided the data into training (90%) and validation (10%).
The training accuracy was 99.8% and the validation accuracy was 100%.
We have designed and implemented a three-class classifier that takes lemon images with a model using deep learning convolutional neural networks.
The proposed approach achieves promising results, notably a validation accuracy of 100%.
We believe that the more images we have, the better the results will be.

A new era for our species started in 1945: with the terrifying demonstration of the power of the atom bomb in Hiroshima and Nagasaki, Japan, the potential global catastrophic consequences of human technology could no longer be ignored.

Within the field of global catastrophic and existential risk, nuclear war is one of the more iconic scenarios, although significant uncertainties remain about its likelihood and potential destructive magnitude.
The risk posed to humanity from nuclear weapons is not static.
In tandem with geopolitical and cultural changes, technological innovations could have a significant impact on how the risk of the use of nuclear weapons changes over time.
Increasing attention has been given in the literature to the impact of digital technologies, and in particular autonomy and machine learning, on nuclear risk.
Most of this attention has focused on 'first-order' effects: the introduction of technologies into nuclear command-and-control and weapon-delivery systems.

This essay focuses instead on higher-order effects: those that stem from the introduction of such technologies into more peripheral systems, with a more indirect (but no less real) effect on nuclear risk.
The risks of these higher-order effects can be divided into two categories.

In the first category are new vulnerabilities in the trusted computing base (TCB) of nuclear deterrence due to the introduction of machine learning into nuclear command, control, communications, computers, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (NC4ISR) systems.
The TCB of a computer system is responsible for enforcing a security policy.

Nuclear deterrence presumably requires a security policy that always allows authorized personnel to detect threats that call for a nuclear response and launch a nuclear response, while never allowing unauthorized personnel to launch nuclear weapons.

The second category of risks consists of novel and amplified threats from the use of autonomy and machine learning in the planning and execution of cyber operations and influence campaigns against nuclear weapon systems and associated personnel.
Both of these categories expand and amplify existing threats, rather than introduce entirely new categories of threat.
Computer systems are susceptible to attack.
They rely on many lines of code that contain numerous opportunities for developers to make a mistake or fail to consider all possible implications, introducing vulnerabilities.
Responses to this computer security threat have evolved over the decades, from pre-deployment testing to formal guarantees that certain parts of code do not contain specific kinds of vulnerability.
Another powerful practice is to limit the 'attack surface' of a system, which can be done by restricting functionality or introducing authority restrictions.
However, some of these security practices limit autonomy, which requires a high level of functionality and integration with numerous inputs.
The challenge of maintaining computer security against digital attacks is even harder for machine learning than for autonomy.
Machine learning approaches seek to bring about correct behavior through analysis of large amounts of data, but the learned behaviors cannot be scrutinized to the same degree as rule-based systems.
A broad range of models trained through machine learning are susceptible to a new kind of vulnerability, termed 'adversarial examples'.
Nuclear deterrence works to counter threats of either nuclear or large-scale conventional attack through the transparency of its posture.
It relies on an always/never alert status: always ready to be executed via legitimate authority, and never subject to compromise.
Cyber operations, like other covert actions, rely on stealth and exploit vulnerabilities unknown to the target states.
Increasingly, cyber vulnerabilities challenge nuclear deterrence because nuclear-armed states may not know that their capabilities have been impaired.
This can lead to either a false sense of confidence or an overblown sense of vulnerability that encourages pre-emptive action.
The erosion of credibility due to these uncertainties undermines the overarching aim of deterring conflict.
The first class of policy responses involve actions that a nuclear-armed state can take unilaterally to reduce the risks that it is exposed to from digital threats.
By making itself more secure, such a state also helps maintain the deterrence relationships that it has in place.
Overall, knowledge of potential exploits and steps to avoid them, detect them and address them must be in place.
The integration of information and communications technology (ICT) systems into NC4ISR should be restricted.
The nuclear-armed states should be mindful of the potential threats and take proactive action to harden systems.
Good practice should be codified and widely dispersed to relevant personnel.
Contingency protocols should be set up, tested and enforced.

The introduction of autonomy and machine learning currently cannot be achieved without introducing new vulnerabilities that undermine the always/never alert status and the credibility of nuclear deterrence.
Therefore, their integration into NC3 and NC4ISR systems should be avoided.

In addition to unilateral action that can be taken by nuclear-armed states to reduce vulnerabilities and prepare for attacks, a second method for not increasing existential risk is to develop and institutionalize international norms and coordination mechanisms.

There are three domains of particular relevance: establishing an international norm prohibiting targeting of NC4ISR systems, promoting a norm against the weaponization of autonomy and machine learning, and sharing cybersecurity best practices.
In Bourgeois equality, Deidre Nansen McCloskey argues, as advertised in the book's subtitle, that 'Ideas, not capital or institutions, enriched the world'.
This ambitious historical project takes its position in opposition to the political left and right.

McCloskey understands the left to reflect the opinion that accumulated capital enriched the bourgeois class by exploiting the working class who will only be included in the capitalist vision of perpetual accumulation as a result of state mandated redistribution.
She understands the right to be the contemporary neo-institutionalists who argue that economic growth will be achieved with the appropriate incentives to reward rational action.

McCloskey's argument is primarily historical, spanning the seventeenth through twentieth centuries, focusing on the European invention of capitalism and the attendant bourgeois virtues of prudence, temperance, and justice.
The strength of the project is its revisitation of the ideals and development of classical liberalism.
Its weakness is McCloskey's failure to engage with or recognize that markets and rationality are historically contextualized cultural forms.

McCloskey's initial task is to convince readers that economic growth under modern capitalism, dating from late-eighteenth century, was spectacular and resulted in a world in which 'many of us shot up the blade of a hockey stick'.

By this, she means that a period of Great Enrichment characterizes the nineteenth and twentieth centuries so that many people worldwide experienced abundance to an extent unimaginable and unachievable in the previous centuries.
Her writing is imaginative and blunt, seeking to persuade more by carefully dispersed facts and rhetorical flourish than a comprehensive numeric defense.

Evidence includes observations such as that 'The upper middle of the present-day seven billion—perhaps two billion, double the population of the world in 1800—live in countries in the mold of Greece or Taiwan or Israel' where the income is over $80 per day.

For those unconvinced of the broadly spread enrichment of modern capitalism, McCloskey points out that 'The English colonists in North America at first lived on $2 a day... Yet by 2011 the average resident of the United States consumed, correctly for inflation, $132, sixty-six times more housing, food, education, furniture than in 1690'.
McCloskey argues that the cost of living goes down for everyone regardless of socioeconomic status due to the efficiency of production in a free market system.
I appreciate McCloskey's defense of idealism in the form of ethical principles, as opposed to Marxist materialism, or a conservative realism deferring to brute power.

She seeks to recapture the role of ethics and innovation as ends in themselves that cannot be reduced to or transformed into a profit motive or incentives characteristic of the contemporary neoliberal practice.
By the 'neo-institutional' school she refers to the rational choice approach developed by Nobel Laureate economist Douglass C. North.
According to this view, agents maximize expected utility, and nothing else.
Effective institutions impose the appropriate incentive structures to drive economic growth through mutually beneficial transactions.
However, McCloskey observes that 'The neo-institutionalist economists have not really taken on the idea that ethical ideas can matter independently (sometimes) from incentives'.

In the remainder of this review, I invite McCloskey to reconsider whether the game theoretic neo-institutionalist school is better understood to range across the political spectrum from right to left.
Let us consider a two by two matrix, with left vs. right as columns, and materialism vs. idealism as rows.
McCloskey describes the Marxist and social welfarist left as being materialist, and the neo-institutionalist game theoretic economists as the right-leaning materialists.
She suggests that the idealist left would be a position akin to Mahatma Gandhi whose principles led him to disdain technology and economic growth in favor of ascetic withdrawal.
McCloskey is a self-described Christian and classic libertarian, although she seems to suggest that her position would be acceptable to secular libertarians.

In view of her acknowledgement of the crucial importance of ideas rather than economic incentives to be the prime mover in human progress toward inclusive betterment, perhaps it is best to refer to her position as one of dialectical libertarianism.
Accounts of intentional agency typically assign beliefs a central role in the genesis of action.
According to them, if someone acts with an intention, the person's action is guided by her beliefs.
The beliefs guide the action by directing the agent towards ways of achieving what she intends.
In this respect, they help rationalize it.
They explain the action by revealing the connection the person saw between what she did and what she intended with it.
Slips are a challenge to this view.
When you slip, you act with an intention, but you inadvertently end up doing something else.
For example, in early January you write the wrong year on a check or, right after moving to a new place, you find yourself driving to the old one.
Surely, you are aware that the year ended and you know that you just moved, but nevertheless, by acting out of habit you behave contrary to what you believe then.
It might be tempting to resist the challenge in two different ways.
One is to claim that slips are not really instances of acting with an intention.
Another is to try to reduce the slip to a doxastic mistake.
Here, I argue both ways of fending off the challenge fail, because they wind up mischaracterizing the mistake.
In the slip the agent acts with an intention, but she does not act guided by her beliefs about how to execute it.
Slips have a rational structure of the sort that accounts of intentional agency are meant to capture.
They exhibit robust and regular patterns, which speaks against them being fortuitous glitches.
Thus, by helping dissociate habitual from other ways of acting intentionally, slips help understand how habits can rationalize what we do.
On January 1st, 2009 police officer Johannes Mehserle shot Oscar Grant dead on a BART platform in Oakland, California.
Mehserle didn't intend to shoot Grant.
Yet, after warning him loud and clear that he would be tased if he continued resisting arrest, the officer pinned him down, drew the weapon, and pulled the trigger once.
Tragically, although Mehserle meant to reach for the taser, he instead reached for his gun.
Slips are common mistakes.
You set out to do something that you normally know how to do, and yet, without changing your mind, you wind up doing something else.
Fortunately, most slips are inconsequential; some are even endearing.
Still, just looking at the institutional responses to these shootings, as opposed to deliberate ones, generates enough to give one pause.
Accounts of intentional agency often assign beliefs an essential role in the production of action.
The approach can be traced back to Aristotle's claim that actions are the conclusions of practical syllogisms.
But it is also common among contemporary action theorists.
The principle of doxastic guidance claims that if someone acts with an intention, what the person does at the time is guided by her beliefs about how to achieve what she intends.
In these cases what forges the connection between intention and action are not one's beliefs but one's acquired habits.
Habits, as understood here, are dispositions to execute intentions in ways which have worked in the past and that have been internalized through a process of rehearsal.
Acting habitually in this sense is one way of acting for reasons.
Slips are exceptions to doxastic guidance.
I have shown that prima facie plausible ways of fending off the challenge do not work.
In the end, the discussion has served to sketch a model of how a psychology of habits can be integrated in an account of intentional agency.
Acting habitually is not antithetic to acting for a reason; habits sometimes function as rationalizing dispositions.
Staying acquainted with the latest technologies remains critical for language teachers as the latter is usually dynamic and gets phased out easily with time.

This necessitates the need for administrators in the education sector, language trainers, and students to work collaboratively and take advantage of the prevailing technologies before they become obsolete.
Such an aspect obligates language trainers specifically and teachers in general to adopt a strategic approach to technology.
This approach encompasses taking a wide array of considerations and principles regarding technology and language learning, language teaching, and language use.

To critically analyze technological evolution in language learning.

As it emerged from philosophical analyses and cognitive research, most concepts exhibit typicality effects, and resist the efforts of defining them in terms of necessary and sufficient conditions.
This holds also in the case of many medical concepts.

This is a problem for the design of computer science ontologies, since knowledge representation formalisms commonly adopted in this field do not allow for the representation of concepts in terms of typical traits.
The need of representing concepts in terms of typical traits concerns almost every domain of real world knowledge, including medical domains.
In particular, in this article we take into account the domain of mental disorders, starting from the DSM-5 descriptions of some specific disorders.
We favour a hybrid approach to concept representation, in which ontology-oriented formalisms are combined with a geometric representation of knowledge based on conceptual space.
As a preliminary step to apply our proposal to mental disorder concepts, we started to develop an OWL ontology of the schizophrenia spectrum, which is as close as possible to the DSM-5 descriptions.
In philosophy and cognitive sciences, different theories about the nature of concepts have been proposed.
According to the traditional view, known as 'classical', concepts can be simply defined in terms of sets of necessary and sufficient conditions.

This theory was dominant until the mid'70s, when philosophical analyses and experimental results showed that, for most common-sense concepts, this position does not hold since conceptual structures are mainly characterized by 'typical' category membership cues and are organized in human mind in terms of prototypes.
Since then, different positions and theories on the nature of concepts have been proposed to explain aspects concerning conceptual 'typicality'.
Usually, they are grouped into three main classes: prototype views, exemplar views, and theory-theories.

The case of some medical concepts, such as the general concept of DISEASE and various individual disease concepts, shows the same problems presented by most common-sense concepts, as they can hardly be represented in terms of individually necessary and jointly sufficient conditions.

Faced with the issues raised by attempts to find a traditional definition for the general concept of DISEASE, some philosophers of medicine have proposed to regard the concept of DISEASE and those of individual diseases as non-classical ones.
In this vein, new theories based on family resemblances, prototypes, or exemplars have been proposed.
These views are different: embracing the family resemblances theory implies that there is no specific set of properties that individual diseases must meet to some degree.
Nevertheless, they are often conflated or muddled in the relevant literature.
In the last decades, the problem of concept representation received a great deal of attention within the field of artificial intelligence, particularly in knowledge representation.
In the AI tradition, an ontology is constituted by a specific vocabulary used to describe a certain reality, plus a set of explicit assumptions regarding the intended meaning of the vocabulary words.
The representation languages adopted for the development of formal ontologies stemmed from structured inheritance semantic networks.
These formalisms are known today as description logics (DLs), and the main formal ontological languages such as OWL belong to this class.
DLs can perform a series of automatic inferences, such as categorization, classification, and consistency checking.
However, Tarskian semantics is fully compositional, and typicality effects are hard to accommodate with compositionality.
As a consequence, DLs do not allow the representation of concepts in prototypical terms.
This strong bias towards the representation of concepts in terms of necessary and/or sufficient conditions alone is a problem in the field of biomedical ontologies.
Most of them are conditioned by the adoption of formalisms that do not allow to represent concepts in typical terms.

As a preliminary step to implement a system based on the above described conceptual architecture, we are currently developing a formal ontology that tries to overcome some limitations of the existing ontological representations of individual mental disorders.

Our assumption that the general concept of MENTAL DISORDER and the various concepts of individual mental disorders should be treated as non-classical ones is preliminarily tested by developing an ontology based on the OWL-DL dialect.
The goal of the first phase was identifying, organizing, and structuring all the main concepts of the domain.
We focused on the chapter of Schizophrenia Spectrum only and defined relevant concepts and properties through a glossary written in natural language.
The Schizophrenia_Spectrum ontology that we have developed is currently composed of 58 classes, 5 properties, and 191 axioms.
The top-level classes chosen by the adopted modelling allow that each mental disorder might be identified through quite different sets of symptoms.
The current version of the ontology is still subject to revisions and extensions.

In the present paper, we shall discuss the notion of prototype and show its benefits.
First, we shall argue that the prototypes of common-sense concepts are necessary for making prompt and reliable categorisations and inferences.

However, the features constituting the prototype of a particular concept are neither necessary nor sufficient conditions for determining category membership; in this sense, the prototype might lead to conclusions regarded as wrong from a theoretical perspective.
That being said, the prototype remains essential to handling most ordinary situations and helps us to perform important cognitive tasks.
To exemplify this point, we shall focus on disease concepts.
Our analysis concludes that the prototypical conception of disease is needed to make important inferences from a practical and clinical point of view.
Moreover, it can still be compatible with a classical definition of disease, given in terms of necessary and sufficient conditions.
In philosophy of language, the term 'stereotype' was introduced by Hilary Putnam.
He famously used the notion of stereotype to account for a speaker's semantic competence, which is identified with her knowledge of the stereotypes associated with words.
To put it briefly, a stereotype is a standardized description of features of the kind that are typical, or 'normal', or at any rate stereotypical.
According to Putnam, a stereotype is thus an oversimplified theory of a word's extension that all competent speakers should know.
However, knowing the stereotype does not suffice to know the meaning of a word or to fully grasp the concept associated with it.
The notion of stereotype is often compared or confused with that of prototype.
The latter notion has been introduced by Eleonor Rosch to account for the typicality effects that are exhibited by many common-sense concepts.
Rosch's psychological experiments showed how common-sense concepts do not obey the requirements of the classical theory.
Rather, concepts exhibit typicality effects: some members of a category are considered better instances than others.
A prototype is an ideal entity that does not necessarily coincide with any real individual.

The notion of stereotype was developed by Putnam in close relationship with his particular conception of semantic meaning, while the notion of prototype was developed by Rosch to account for typicality effects.
Typicality effects in categorisation and, in general, in category representation are crucial for human cognition.
It is not easy to say under what conditions we should say that somebody knows the concept DOG.

However, if a person does not know that, for example, dogs usually bark, that they typically have four legs, that their body is covered with fur, then we should probably conclude that this person does not grasp the concept DOG.
Nevertheless, all of these pieces of information are neither necessary nor sufficient conditions for being a dog.
The majority of everyday concepts behave in this way.
For most concepts, a classical definition in terms of necessary and sufficient conditions is not available.
Moreover, it may be that we know the classical definition of a concept, but typical/prototypical knowledge still plays a central role in many cognitive tasks.
Human beings have a strong inclination to reason in prototypical terms.
The conjunction fallacy consists in failing to realise that a conjunction is always less probable than its conjuncts.
From the standpoint of a theory of reasoning, this is a paradigmatic case of a systematic error.

However, if we consider the problem from the point of view of a theory of concepts, the conjunction fallacy can be interpreted as an example of the strong tendency of human subjects to resort to prototypical information in categorisation.

The use of prototypical knowledge in cognitive tasks such as categorisation is related to the constraints that concern every finite agent that has limited access to the knowledge relevant for a given task.

Focusing on a contentious and debated concept in philosophy of medicine, that of DISEASE, we shall exemplify how prototypical concepts have a positive and important role from a practical point of view.
At the same time, we shall maintain that their 'negative' side makes them compatible with the possibility that a classical definition of the concept of DISEASE might eventually be found.

We wish to show that, even if the prototypical DISEASE may eventually lead to categorisations considered wrong from the point of view of theoretical medicine, it is still essential for promptly and reliably handling most ordinary situations.
The prototypical concept of DISEASE can be regarded as highly valuable and beneficial.

However, as a prototypical concept does not pretend to exactly characterise the concept of DISEASE, it is still compatible with the possibility that the concept of DISEASE would be definable in terms of necessary and sufficient conditions.
The prototypical concept of DISEASE would consist of both central and marginal examples.
Conditions such as tuberculosis, pneumonia or breast cancer are relatively prototypical examples for most individuals.
On the other hand, micromastia, cellulite or alcoholism may easily count as dubious conditions for many individuals.

The prototypical characterisation of disease may lead to wrong characterisations from the point of view of theoretical medicine, however, it is still very useful to sort out pragmatic and clinical tasks in a prompt and reliable way.
To sum up, disease concepts exhibit typicality effects that can be successfully explained in terms of prototypes.
The prototypical characterisation of disease may lead to wrong characterisations from the point of view of theoretical medicine.
However, it is still very useful to sort out pragmatic and clinical tasks in a prompt and reliable way.
This means that the prototypical and the classical characterisations of the general concept of disease might still be compatible, as they respond to different cognitive tasks.
John Searle offers what he thinks to be a reasonable scientific approach to the understanding of consciousness.

I argue that Searle is demanding nothing less than a Kuhnian-type revolution with respect to how scientists should study consciousness given his rejection of the subject-object distinction and affirmation of mental causation.
Few questions concerning the human condition have been asked by serious thinkers and answered in diametrically opposed ways as the question 'What is the nature of mind?'

There are at least three distinct but related questions potentially being asked when this question is posed: 'How does this entity, putatively labeled 'mind,' come into existence?', 'What kind of substance (or thing) is this entity called mind?', and 'Is there any kind of scientific explanation of this entity called mind?'
Searle has attempted to provide answers to some of the questions noted above about MCS that attack certain central assumptions shared by many members of the scientific community.
His conclusion is that our current scientific practices and assumptions cannot hope to understand the nature of MCS, but that he has an approach that may prove rather efficacious.
Kuhn explains that 'normal science' is the solving of problems by scientists through shared paradigms.
Paradigms are agreed upon or accepted methodologies that are used by members of a scientific community as they attempt to unravel specific problems within their respective sub-fields.

Churchland suggests that a sophisticated enough neuroscience will provide all the answers we will ever need to understand psychological terms such as mind, consciousness, subjective experience, desire, belief, and emotion.
Eliminative materialists argue that psychological phenomena/events do not exist.
Searle offers that we could redefine 'consciousness' to mean the neurobiological causes of our subjective experiences.
However, he insists that we need a word to refer to ontologically subjective phenomena of awareness or sentience.
Searle claims that consciousness refers to those states of sentience or awareness that typically begin when we wake from a dreamless sleep.
He distinguishes between objective-subjective distinctions in both epistemic and ontological senses.
Searle considers MCS to be a quality that emerges from the complex interaction of certain neurobiological and neurochemical processes.
He argues that consciousness cannot be deduced or calculated from the sheer physical structure of the neurons without some additional account of the causal relations between them.
Searle's request for a change in methodology by scientists is significant.
He asks the scientific community to abandon the subject-object and appearance-reality distinctions that are integral to their methodology.

If scientists are to embrace Searle's emergent1 as the correct account of MCS, they will have to do so at the expense of rejecting the subject/object distinction and the appearance/reality distinction.
Searle has not provided persuasive arguments for the scientific community to abandon their current methodology of studying MCS.
The debate in the legal reasoning subfield of jurisprudence has paid so far scant attention to the work of those making full use of formal and informal argumentative techniques.
It is common to find philosophical reflections where the focus is on legal reasoning as a form of practical reasoning, of rhetorical and legal narrative analysis, or of argumentative analysis.
However, in the field of general argumentation theory new developments have emerged which intersect with work in closely related fields such as computational argumentation and narrative analysis.

In this article we critically engage with the literature and suggest our own take on the kind of methodological choices which are available to the legal theorist, and exemplify our approach via the analysis of a case study.
In Argumentation Studies (AS) three perspectives compete for the attention of scholars: (Informal) Logic, Dialectic, and Rhetoric.
Originally, arguments were the topic of formal logic, with its emphasis on deductive and inductive reasoning.

The Informal Logic movement originated in the 70s because of a dissatisfaction with the state of the discipline regarding the common use of language in everyday life as well as in specialised fields such as law and social scientific disciplines.
Several informal forms of reasoning which are neither deductive nor inductive became the focus of this newly-born specialty.
Instead of listing all these forms, Bickenbach and Davies put under the 'practical reasoning' label all those modes of argumentation which are neither deductive nor inductive.
The study of practical reasoning overlaps with investigations in the philosophy and methodology of the social sciences.
The study of practical reasoning in the philosophical area of action theory does not necessarily include a focus on ethical aspects and normative reasons for action.
The mainstream paradigm, also called neo-Humean, is eminently instrumental in its focus, with an emphasis on the individual and psychological aspects of practical deliberation.
In this article the focus is instead on practical argumentation as an external, social phenomenon, in both its normative and empirical aspects since legal decisions have a practical orientation.
Returning now to dialectical approaches to legal reasoning, the key figure in this computing-influenced sub-field is Douglas Walton.
Walton distinguishes between two models of theoretical and practical reasoning and acting: the BDI and the commitment models.
The commitment model maintains that the major premise should indicate the agent's goals described as normative commitments.
This model is relevant for the analysis and evaluation, being based on publicly available data, such as court proceedings.
The socio-legal literature has put particular emphasis on scripts, which are commonly known ways of carrying out everyday activities.
Scripts are just one example of the wider narrative approach used to complement the argumentation one.
Story schemes will be used to show the relationships between actions and events.
Complementing the argumentation approach with the narrative approach would lead to rich explanations of actions and events.
We turn now to a specific legal issue, the admissibility of expert evidence in criminal trials.
Many forensic science methods routinely used in the criminal courts are of unproven validity.
Awareness of the shaky foundations of much forensic science evidence has led to debate among legal scholars about whether such evidence should be admissible in a criminal jury trial.
The conventional common-law view is that the weight of expert evidence is a matter for the jury.
In order to understand how the above discussion of practical reasoning is relevant to evidence law, it is important to clarify the nature of the law of evidence in common-law systems.
The jury's task is to evaluate the evidence and return a verdict.
The test that English and Welsh juries are instructed to apply is whether they are 'sure' of guilt.
The judge decides what evidence can properly be put before the jury, evaluating its relevance and probative value.
The issues surrounding knowledge, justification and causality have been extensively discussed by both the philosophical and evidence law communities.

We have argued that it is crucial to distinguish between practical argumentation concerning the probative value and admissibility of evidence, and argumentation aimed at establishing the truth about past events.
If this distinction is kept clearly in view, both argumentation theory and theories of narrative can shed significant light on current debates about evidence law and practice.
The global Covid-19 pandemic has significantly impacted the way we live our lives.
In addition to health and economic effects, consequences for the ways that we work have been dramatic and persistent.
Office cubicles and boardroom tables made way for Zoom meetings and email exchanges, with further and ongoing changes to be navigated for some time yet.

Now that many countries have achieved significant vaccination rates, a return to 'business as usual' is considered by some to be necessary and perhaps long overdue, prompting discussion about a return to in-person office work after the rapid and ad hoc shift to remote working arrangements.
However, many employees who experienced benefits from working remotely have expressed reluctance about returning to the office, and responses amongst employers have been mixed.
Some of the largest and most influential global companies are navigating the issue in real time and in the public eye, and they are coming to strikingly disparate positions.
Divergent approaches are evident even amongst dominant firms in just the technology sector.

Apple employees, for example, disapproved of a policy that would require them to return to the office for three days a week, expressing a desire to instead maintain a more flexible approach that allows more home-based work.
Google employees were initially threatened with pay cuts if they opted to continue working from home, although that position has been revised since.

In contrast, Facebook and Twitter have been supportive of maintaining remote work, perhaps indicating that for some companies at least, there are competitive and cost advantages to a reduction in office work.
To motivate the need for a new approach, let us first survey the approaches open to employers for deciding whether, and how, employees ought to return to the office.
In his recent book The Future of the Office, Peter Cappelli identifies four basic possibilities.
First, employees could be instructed to return to the office when it is safe to do so.
Second, staff could be allowed to continue working away from the office; in other words, that arrangements initially considered temporary become permanent.
A third option is a hybrid approach, where some staff would return to the office while others continue working remotely.
Finally, Cappelli proposes a fourth, the so-called 'waiting to see' approach.
The mixed and conflicting opinions about the future of remote office work entail questions about both how decisions ought to be made and what factors are relevant to making them.

Rather than deciding such matters in advance, our proposal is to focus first on understanding the purpose of an organisation broadly and second on the purpose of the jobs within that organisation that incorporate office work.
The purpose-focused approach draws upon the timeless work of Aristotle.
According to him, everything has a 'telos', which is its ultimate purpose, end, or goal.
Understanding this, we realise that an attempt to utilise a knife made of jelly to cut some bread will inevitably end in failure.

Establishing the fundamental purpose of the organisation and the contribution of each job to that purpose is the crucial first step for reorienting discussions about a return to in-person office work.

Rather than locating reasons for one's position amongst personal preferences or perceptions of how the job has been performed previously, the discussion will be about how the job contributes to the organisation's fundamental purpose.
If that contribution requires being present in an office, then the threshold decision is made, and the discussion can move on to the conditions associated with a return to the office.
One essential trait of successful managers is the ability to decide how much detailed analysis is required to make a good decision.
Taking the case of the design engineer, it might be enough for her manager to know that she is typically well organised and competent in the use of Zoom to stay in touch with her peers.
By contrast, the case of the Training Manager might require a great deal of empirical information to make the policy and define exceptions to it.
If our focus shifts to the socio-economic context in which work is conducted, then it becomes apparent that the public policy and regulatory environments are relevant, too.
The relationship is not uni-directional: decisions about the nature and conditions of a return to office work across industries and whole economies will impact upon public policy, too.
Public policy has an incredibly important role in shaping societies and workplaces.

Decisions about whether and how to return to in-person office work are urgent, significant for a range of organisational and social reasons, and likely to be revisited as the Covid pandemic progresses.
Taking our lead from Aristotle's concept of telos, we propose instead a methodology that is strictly purpose oriented.

By aligning the decision about a return to work with the fundamental purpose of work, individual roles, and a business overall, it is possible to ensure that new work arrangements will be consistent with the organisation's reason for being.
Branching-time is a popular theory of time that is intended to account for the openness of the future.
Generally, branching-time models the openness of the future by positing a multiplicity of concrete alternative futures mirroring all the possible ways the future could unfold.
A distinction is drawn in the literature among branching-time theories: those that make use of moment-based structures and those that employ history-based ones.
In this paper, I introduce and discuss a particular kind of openness relative to the possibility that time ends (Doomsday).
I then show that whereas moment-based branching structures cannot represent this kind of openness, history-based structures can account for it.
The conclusion is that history-based structures score a point over moment-based ones.
Throughout the paper, I will make use of the temporal Ockhamist semantics.

Although the points I am going to make do not depend on the nature of the Ockhamist semantics, I will adopt the Ockhamist semantics as it is a common and convenient way to formalize modal-temporal claims in the context of branching time.
In this section, I will quickly recap some of its main tenets, as well as two important principles of branching-time structures, viz. no backward branching and historical connectedness.
To start, let us introduce a temporal language L which includes an infinite set of non-tensed atomic sentence letters, the standard connectives, and the temporal operators.

Next, a Branching-Time Model (BTM) is defined as an ordered triple, where T is a non-empty set of moments, ≤ is a binary, transitive, and reflexive at-least-as-earlier-than relation over T, and T RUE is a two place-function that assigns either true or false to couples of moments/atomic sentence letters.
Histories are then defined as maximally ordered sets of related moments of T-intuitively, a history is one of the many possible complete developments of the world.
There is an open debate on what should be preferred between moment-based and history-based branching structures.

One of the aspects of the debate revolves around which one between the two structures fares better with respect to representing scenarios that, from an intuitive viewpoint, constitute genuine metaphysical possibilities.
Consider the following two sentences.
Inevitably, if today there is life on earth, then either this is the last day or the last day will come.
At any possible day at which there is life on earth, it is possible that there will be life on earth the following day.
Øhrstrøm and Hasle judge these sentences to be compatible.
If the two are indeed compatible and hold at all pairs, there could then be a branching structure where both sentences are true at all pairs.
However, in history-based structures, the set of related moments can be excluded by the set of histories, thereby avoiding contradictions and making the sentences compatible.
In this section, I am going to provide an example that seems to score a clear point in favor of history-based structures.
The scenario described in the example is about the end of time itself, i.e. Doomsday.
The future can be open in at least two ways: absolute openness and relative openness.
In the case of absolute openness, it is open at a moment whether Doomsday will come.
In the case of relative openness, it is inevitable that time will end but it is open when it will.
However, consider this further case of Doomsday openness.
At one specific moment, it is open whether the world continues or ends right at that moment.
This kind of openness is distinct from absolute and relative openness.
It is a genuine metaphysical possibility that at a very specific moment, it is indeterminate whether the world itself continues or not.
To model this case of present openness, we need to introduce broken histories.
A broken-at-m history is a subset of moments that has a last moment and also has later moments according to the fundamental earlier-than relation.
By making use of broken histories, we can represent the scenario of present openness.
The present openness scenario is different in nature from the previous examples.
In that discussion, one of the questions was whether or not we should remove from the set of histories of the model a set of moments that would normally count as a history.
In the present openness scenario, what is required is that we add a history.
The scenario of present openness seems to be a genuine metaphysical possibility.
However, we need broken histories to model it, and broken histories can be admitted only if we adopt history-based structures.
Moment-based structures simply cannot make room for broken histories.
It follows that history-based structures can represent a genuine metaphysical possibility that cannot be represented in the framework of moment-based structures.
